public_rationale: He forecast that enterprise AI spending continues for now, until firms broadly see they can cut costs, first by moving to open-source models and then by not using them at all. He set no deadline. A September 2026 enterprise survey reported by Techstrong says cost is the main reason firms adopt open-weight models, and 60% of production users moved some workloads off proprietary models. That fits his first stage. But 93% said their proprietary use keeps growing, and nothing shows enterprises dropping models. Two months after the post, the evidence neither completes his sequence nor refutes an open-ended forecast.
limitations: The survey covers only 200 respondents and measures token share, not spending.
The publication date of the Techstrong page is not shown.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: While 'doing AI' is still rewarded, enterprise AI spending will continue until everybody realizes they can likely cut a large amount of costs, first by moving to open-source models and then by not using them at all.
conditions: while doing AI still feels good and gets rewarded

statement.excerpt: Yet we’re still in the period where “doing AI” feels good and gets rewarded (or not doing AI gets punished), which means the spend will continue until everybody realizes they can likely cut a shit ton of costs, first by moving to open source models, then not using them at all, because even open source is expensive and questionably-useful.

from_speaker: "until everybody realizes they can likely cut a shit ton of costs"
"first by moving to open source models"
premise: "we're still in the period where 'doing AI' feels good and gets rewarded"
our_interpretation: My reading is a sequence forecast about enterprise AI spending in general. Spending keeps going for now. Later, enterprises broadly come to see that they can cut costs, first by moving to open-source models and then by dropping models altogether.
The post presents 'doing AI gets rewarded' as the current state, not as a condition to test. I do not score it as an antecedent.
'Everybody' is rhetorical. I read it as a broad, market-wide shift, not every single firm.
He gave no deadline, so the forecast is open-ended. A finite period of continued spending cannot refute it, because he says spending continues until the realization arrives.
criteria.support_condition: Dated evidence after 2026-08-25 that enterprises broadly cut AI model spending for cost reasons: first a widespread move from proprietary to open-source models to save money, then a broad move to stop using models. Evidence of only the first stage would partly support the forecast but would not settle it.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Because there is no deadline, no finite record can contradict it outright. It would be weakened by sustained evidence of broad enterprise spending growth on proprietary models with no turn toward open-source substitution or abandonment for cost reasons.

evidence.excerpt: Among enterprises running open-weight models in production, 60% have transferred some workloads from proprietary offerings. However, 93% report that their proprietary model usage continues to grow.
evidence.locator: paragraph beginning 'In short, the open-weight vs. proprietary model issue'
evidence.explanation: Some enterprises are moving workloads to open models, which fits the first stage. But proprietary use is still growing, so spending continues and there is no sign of abandonment. The page shows no publication date. The survey ran in September 2026, so available_at is approximate.

evidence.excerpt: The cost of AI inference is a key driver of enterprise interest in open-weight models. Cost savings were cited by 69% of production users and 67% of organizations conducting pilots.
evidence.locator: section 'Cost Drives Adoption, Security Slows Deployment', paragraph 1
evidence.explanation: Cost savings drive the open-model shift. This is consistent with his first stage, but it does not show that enterprises are dropping models.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Broad, dated spending data showing that enterprises cut AI model spend for cost reasons, through open-source substitution followed by widespread stopping of use.
